column2: To 'interpret' a confidence interval for a population proportion, you must:
column3: State the confidence level and describe the interval as capturing the parameter in context
column4: Calculate the margin of error by subtracting the lower bound from the upper bound
column5: Verify that the three required conditions for inference have all been fully satisfied
column6: Convert the interval endpoints into counts by multiplying each one by the population size

column2: Which interpretation of a 95% CI of (0.31, 0.47) for a population proportion is correct?
column3: We are 95% confident that the interval from 0.31 to 0.47 captures the population proportion
column4: There is a 95% probability that the true population proportion falls between 0.31 and 0.47
column5: Exactly 95% of all individuals in the population have a value between 0.31 and 0.47
column6: The sample proportion is 95% likely to change by no more than 0.08 in repeated samples

column2: The phrase 'We are 95% confident' in a confidence interval interpretation refers to:
column3: The long-run capture rate of the method — about 95% of such intervals would contain the parameter
column4: The probability that this one specific calculated interval successfully contains the true parameter
column5: The percentage of individuals in the sample who actually have the characteristic being studied
column6: The likelihood that a future sample would produce a proportion within this exact same interval

column2: Once a specific confidence interval has been calculated, that interval captures the true proportion:
column3: With probability 1 if the parameter is inside the interval, or probability 0 if it is not
column4: With probability 0.95 if a 95% confidence level was used to construct the interval
column5: With an unknown probability that depends on whether the conditions were properly met
column6: With probability 0.50 since it either captures the parameter or it does not capture it

column2: In repeated random sampling with the same sample size, approximately 95% of 95% CIs will:
column3: Capture the true population proportion, though any single interval may or may not succeed
column4: Produce identical lower and upper bounds because the sampling method stays the same
column5: Have margin of error values that fall within 5% of the first interval that was calculated
column6: Contain the sample proportion that was observed in the original sample from the study

column2: Which of the following is a common misconception about confidence intervals?
column3: There is a 95% probability that the true proportion is located within this particular interval
column4: About 95% of intervals constructed from repeated samples will capture the true parameter
column5: Any individual confidence interval either contains the true population proportion or it does not
column6: The confidence level describes the long-run success rate of the confidence interval procedure

column2: A proper confidence interval interpretation must reference the specific population because:
column3: The interval estimates a real-world quantity about a specific group, not just an abstract number
column4: The AP exam formula sheet requires a population name to determine which formula applies here
column5: Intervals that do not mention a population will always produce margins of error that are too large
column6: The numerical value of the confidence level changes depending on which population is described

column2: A student writes: '95% of students in our sample scored between 0.62 and 0.78.' This is:
column3: Incorrect — a CI estimates a population parameter, not the range of individual sample values
column4: Correct — this is the standard template for interpreting a confidence interval for a proportion
column5: Incorrect — the percentage should be stated as 5% rather than 95% based on the significance level
column6: Correct — but only if the Large Counts condition has been properly verified using calculations

column2: After calculating a 90% CI, a student says 'there is a 90% chance our interval got it right.' This is:
column3: Incorrect — the interval either contains the parameter or it does not; 90% is the long-run rate
column4: Correct — this is a reasonable informal interpretation of what the 90% confidence level means
column5: Incorrect — the correct probability should actually be stated as 10% rather than 90% for this
column6: Correct — but only when the sample was selected using a properly randomized sampling method

column2: When interpreting a confidence interval, you should NOT interpret the confidence level unless:
column3: The problem specifically asks you to explain what the stated confidence level means in context
column4: The confidence level that was used is anything lower than 95% confidence for the procedure
column5: The sample size is smaller than 30 observations, which makes the margin of error unreliable
column6: The 10% condition was not satisfied, which requires adjusting the confidence level reported

column2: Students who attempt to interpret the confidence level without being asked often:
column3: Make errors that lose points, because the confidence level interpretation is frequently stated wrong
column4: Earn extra credit, because interpreting the level shows a deeper understanding of the concept
column5: Are penalized only if the interpretation is technically correct but lacking specific real context
column6: Receive full credit regardless, because any attempt to discuss the confidence level is valued

column2: A confidence interval for a population proportion provides an interval of values that:
column3: May provide sufficient evidence to support or fail to support a particular claim in context
column4: Proves with absolute certainty whether a specific claim about the population is true or false
column5: Replaces the need for significance testing by giving a definitive answer about any hypothesis
column6: Estimates how many individuals in the sample have the characteristic that is being studied

column2: A 95% CI for a population proportion is (0.54, 0.72). Is there convincing evidence that more than half the population has this characteristic?
column3: Yes — all values in the interval are above 0.50, so less than half is not a plausible outcome
column4: Yes — the sample proportion of 0.63 is clearly larger than 0.50, which is enough by itself
column5: No — the interval does not include the value 0.50 exactly, so we cannot make any conclusion
column6: No — a 95% confidence interval is never sufficient to provide evidence for a claim like this

column2: A 95% CI for a population proportion is (0.43, 0.61). Is there convincing evidence of a majority?
column3: No — the interval includes values below 0.50, so a proportion less than half is still plausible
column4: Yes — the point estimate of 0.52 is above 0.50, which is sufficient evidence of a majority
column5: No — confidence intervals can only estimate parameters and can never be used to evaluate claims
column6: Yes — more than half of the values in the interval are above the 0.50 majority threshold

column2: To justify a claim using a confidence interval, you check whether:
column3: All plausible values in the interval are consistent with the particular claim being evaluated
column4: The sample proportion alone is consistent with the claim, regardless of the interval bounds
column5: The margin of error is smaller than the difference between the claim value and the estimate
column6: The confidence level is high enough to guarantee the claim is true for the entire population

column2: A CI of (0.22, 0.38) is used to evaluate the claim that the proportion is at least 0.40. The conclusion:
column3: The interval does not support the claim because all plausible values fall below 0.40
column4: The interval supports the claim because 0.38 is reasonably close to the value of 0.40
column5: No conclusion can be drawn because the claimed value falls outside the calculated interval
column6: The interval supports the claim because the lower bound of 0.22 is far enough from 0.40

column2: If one or more plausible values in a CI are inconsistent with a claim, then:
column3: There is not convincing evidence for the claim based on the calculated confidence interval
column4: The claim has been proven false and we can state definitively that the opposite is true
column5: The confidence interval needs to be recalculated at a higher confidence level to be useful
column6: There is convincing evidence against the claim, and we should reject it with full certainty

column2: A CI of (0.65, 0.81) is used to evaluate a claim that the proportion exceeds 0.60. The conclusion:
column3: The interval supports the claim because every plausible value in the interval exceeds 0.60
column4: The interval supports the claim because the midpoint of 0.73 is clearly greater than 0.60
column5: The interval does not support the claim because 0.60 is not contained within the interval
column6: The interval supports the claim because at least one of the endpoints is greater than 0.60

column2: Evidence from a confidence interval is 'convincing' for a claim only when:
column3: Every single plausible value within the entire interval is consistent with the stated claim
column4: At least half of the plausible values within the interval are consistent with the stated claim
column5: The sample statistic used to construct the interval is consistent with the claim by itself
column6: The confidence level used is 95% or higher, which automatically makes any evidence convincing

column2: A 95% CI for voter support is (0.48, 0.56). A campaign claims the candidate will win (needs > 50%). Based on the CI:
column3: Not convincing — values like 0.48 and 0.49 are plausible, meaning less than half is possible
column4: Convincing — the point estimate of 0.52 exceeds the 0.50 threshold needed for a majority
column5: Not convincing — a 95% CI is never precise enough to evaluate claims about election outcomes
column6: Convincing — the upper bound of 0.56 is well above 0.50, which supports the win claim

column2: A claim states that fewer than 25% of residents use public transit. A 95% CI is (0.18, 0.29). The CI:
column3: Does not support the claim because 0.29 exceeds 0.25, making 'at least 25%' still plausible
column4: Supports the claim because the point estimate of approximately 0.235 falls below 0.25
column5: Does not support the claim because confidence intervals cannot be used for 'less than' claims
column6: Supports the claim because the lower bound of 0.18 is well below the value of 0.25

column2: A CI of (0.71, 0.85) is evaluated against the claim that the proportion exceeds 0.75. The conclusion:
column3: Not convincing — the value 0.71 is below 0.75, so a proportion under 0.75 is still plausible
column4: Convincing — the midpoint of the interval exceeds 0.75, which is sufficient for the claim
column5: Convincing — 0.75 falls inside the interval, which means the claim is supported by the data
column6: Not convincing — the upper bound would need to exceed 0.90 for this claim to be supported

column2: The relationship between the width of a confidence interval and the margin of error is:

column4: The width of the interval is exactly equal to the margin of error for any confidence interval

column2: When all other factors remain the same, increasing the sample size will:
column3: Decrease the width of the confidence interval by reducing the standard error of p-hat
column4: Increase the width of the confidence interval by introducing more variation from the data
column5: Have no effect on the width because the width depends only on the chosen confidence level

column3: Increase the width of the interval because a larger critical value z-star is required
column4: Decrease the width of the interval because higher confidence means greater overall precision
column5: Have no effect on the interval width since width depends only on the chosen sample size
column6: Increase the standard error of p-hat, which independently increases the margin of error

column2: For a population proportion, the width of the CI is proportional to 1/√n. This means:
column3: Larger samples produce narrower intervals, but with diminishing returns as n increases
column4: Larger samples produce narrower intervals at a constant rate as the sample size grows
column5: Smaller samples produce narrower intervals, because less data means less uncertainty
column6: The sample size has no meaningful impact on the width of the confidence interval

column2: To cut the margin of error in half while keeping the confidence level the same, you must:
column3: Quadruple the sample size, because the margin of error is proportional to one over root n
column4: Double the sample size, because the margin of error decreases at a constant linear rate
column5: Cut the sample size in half, because a smaller sample produces less overall variability

column2: A 90% CI computed from the same data will be _____ compared to a 95% CI:
column3: Narrower — the critical value for 90% confidence is smaller, producing a smaller margin of error
column4: Wider — 90% confidence requires capturing more of the distribution to reach the stated level
column5: The same width — both intervals use the same sample data and have the same standard error

column2: Which combination of changes would produce the narrowest confidence interval for a proportion?
